2026 · arXiv · Benchmarks & Evals

Organizing, Orchestrating, and Benchmarking Agent Skills at Ecosystem Scale

AgentSkillOS organizes decentralized Claude Agent Skill ecosystems of up to 200,000 skills, drawn from a 280,000+-skill marketplace, into a capability tree and composes retrieved skills into DAG-based execution plans, then measures whether any of that structure actually helps on a new 30-task, LLM-judged, Bradley-Terry-ranked benchmark against flat native skill invocation.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Since Anthropic introduced Agent Skills in October 2025 — a skill is a markdown file defining a folder of declarative instructions, executable scripts, and auxiliary resources that an LLM can load at runtime — the format has been adopted across model providers and platforms such as Coze. By late February 2026 more than 280,000 skills were publicly listed on the skillsmp.com marketplace, the overwhelming majority contributed by decentralized, third-party developers. That scale creates two distinct problems the paper says nobody had addressed together: users can't get a global view of what skills exist or how they overlap, making targeted selection hard; and agents themselves have no mechanism for composing several skills into something bigger than any one skill alone, so the paper's own framing is that skills "increasingly become fragmented and isolated contributions" and that "many skills remain underused."

The paper argues existing agent benchmarks don't measure this problem either. Tool-use suites like ToolLLM, API-Bank, Gorilla, and TaskBench, and broader agent benchmarks like AgentBench, GAIA, and TheAgentCompany, confine agents to a small, predefined, finite tool set and score them mainly on binary endpoint success — they don't test open-ended discovery over an enormous, evolving skill space, and they emphasize pass/fail over the qualitative usability of what gets produced. The one benchmark built specifically for Claude-style skills, the concurrent SkillsBench, measures the marginal accuracy gain from adding curated skills to mostly terminal-based tasks, but — per this paper's own reading of it — doesn't test whether an agent can autonomously discover, select, and compose multiple skills, and doesn't cover multi-modal, artifact-rich deliverables.

// how it works

The method

AgentSkillOS splits the problem into an offline organization stage (Manage Skills) and an online task-solving stage (Solve Tasks). In Manage Skills, the ecosystem is organized into a capability tree built by recursive, node-level categorization: starting from a root that is manually fixed into five categories (content creation, data processing, software development, automation, domain-specific), an LLM performs Group Discovery (propose category names for a node's skill set, guided by a branching factor B) and then Skill Assignment (place each skill into one of those categories), splitting any node whose skill count exceeds a per-node capacity threshold C = ⌊1.5B⌋ until every node is within budget. Categories left with exactly one skill get merged back into their nearest neighbor; skills the LLM fails to place get reassigned or dumped into the largest category. When the ecosystem is too large to tree over directly, a usage-frequency queue — ranked by marketplace install count — keeps only the top-K most-used skills (plus any the user has manually added) in the active tree; the rest sit in a "dormant index" retrievable by embedding similarity.

In Solve Tasks, a task-specific agent (i) walks the capability tree layer-by-layer to retrieve a broad candidate set, then deduplicates and ranks it down to the top M = 8 skills; (ii) hands that shortlist to an LLM that decomposes the task into sub-tasks and assembles them into a Directed Acyclic Graph of skill invocations, offering three orchestration strategies — Quality-First (adds preparation/refinement stages to maximize output quality), Efficiency-First (maximizes parallelism, minimizing sequential hops), and Simplicity-First (the minimal DAG in which every node is necessary); and (iii) executes the DAG layer by layer — nodes in the same layer run in parallel, dependent layers run sequentially — with each node's prompt carrying the sub-task, the skill to invoke, upstream artifacts, and the expected output. A completed plan is cached in a "recipe pool" and can be reused directly for future similar task descriptions via embedding similarity, skipping retrieval and orchestration entirely. Capability-tree construction, retrieval, and orchestration all run on claude-opus-4.5; each DAG node is actually executed by the Claude Code Agent SDK running claude-sonnet-4.5.

To evaluate any of this, the authors also had to build their own benchmark, since no existing one fit the open-ended, multi-skill setting. It consists of 30 human-crafted tasks across five categories — Data Computation, Document Creation, Motion Video, Visual Design, and Web Interaction (six tasks each) — each requiring a complete, end-user-facing artifact (PDF, PPTX, DOCX, an HTML page, a video, or generated images) rather than a snippet of code or a QA answer. Tasks were built by first curating real skills from public marketplaces and GitHub, then writing task descriptions and deliverable requirements around them, sometimes requiring a single skill and sometimes cross-composing several. Because outputs arrive in heterogeneous raw formats, a scripted pipeline first converts everything into an "LLM-evaluable" form — documents/slides rendered as page images, HTML pages captured as screenshots, videos sampled into frames with duration/resolution/frame-rate metadata, images resized, text included verbatim up to a length cap. An LLM judge (claude-opus-4.5) then performs pairwise comparison between two systems' artifacts for the same task, run in both presentation orders; if the two orders agree the shared preference is kept, if only one order errors the valid one is used, and if the two orders disagree the outcome is recorded as a tie. Across all pairs of the N compared systems, the resulting win counts fill a matrix W (ties add 0.5 to each side), and a Bradley-Terry model is fit to it by maximum likelihood (the MM algorithm, with Laplace smoothing α = 1) to produce one continuous strength parameter βi per system.

P(i ≻ j) = eβieβi + eβj     Si = βi − βminβmax − βmin × 100 // Bradley-Terry win probability, and the final [0,100] rescaled ranking score S_i — fit separately per ecosystem size, so a "100" at |S|=200 and a "100" at |S|=200K are not the same absolute quality
// what they found

The results

The experiments compare eight configurations across three skill-ecosystem sizes (|S| = 200, 1K, 200K skills): the three AgentSkillOS orchestration variants (Quality-First, Efficiency-First, Simplicity-First); an oracle variant (Quality-First (Oracle), which skips tree retrieval and is handed the benchmark's ground-truth skills directly); three ablations that give the flat, unstructured Claude Code Agent SDK skills without any DAG orchestration (w/ Full Pool = the entire ecosystem, w/ Retrieval = only the tree-retrieved skills, w/ Oracle Skills = the ground-truth skills); and Vanilla, the skill-free Claude Code Agent SDK baseline.

Bradley-Terry ranking scores, rescaled to [0,100] separately within each ecosystem size (100 = top-ranked method for that block, 0 = bottom-ranked; Quality-First and Vanilla hit those endpoints by construction of the rescaling, not because the gap to their nearest rival is fixed).

All three AgentSkillOS variants consistently rank above both baselines at every scale, and Quality-First is the top-ranked method at all three sizes. The more informative number is the gap between Quality-First and its nearest AgentSkillOS rival, Efficiency-First, which narrows as the ecosystem grows — 58.5 at |S|=200 up to 89.0 at |S|=200K. w/ Full Pool (handing the entire skill pool to native, unstructured Claude Code invocation) tells a messier story: its score goes 24.3 → 48.1 → 17.2 across the three sizes — it actually improves from 200 to 1K skills before collapsing at 200K, rather than declining monotonically. The paper's own reading of this is that "an increasing fraction of skills becomes invisible to the agent" as the pool grows, nullifying the benefit of a bigger ecosystem — a claim the 200K endpoint supports, though the improvement at 1K over 200 isn't explained. Per-category radar charts (fitting a separate Bradley-Terry model to each of the five task categories) show the three AgentSkillOS variants forming large, well-rounded polygons at every scale, while w/ Full Pool and Vanilla trace small, lopsided shapes with specific weak categories (e.g. Vanilla scores a 0/4/20 win/tie/loss record in Web Interaction at |S|=200K).

An ablation isolates what tree retrieval and DAG orchestration each contribute, comparing Quality-First against the four other configurations across all 30 tasks. Quality-First beats w/ Full Pool decisively at every scale (21 wins / 2 ties / 7 losses out of 30 at |S|=200; 18/3/9 at 1K; 21/2/7 at 200K) and beats w/ Retrieval just as clearly (22/5/3, 15/7/8, 18/5/7), confirming that tree-based retrieval alone, without DAG composition, is not enough. It also beats w/ Oracle Skills — the flat agent handed the perfect skill set with no orchestration — by a solid margin at every scale (18/6/6, 17/7/6, 19/3/8), the paper's central point that structured composition, not just skill availability, unlocks the skill ecosystem's value. Against Quality-First (Oracle), though, tree-retrieved Quality-First actually has more losses than wins at every ecosystem size: 10 wins / 6 ties / 14 losses at |S|=200 (net −4), 11/7/12 at 1K (net −1), 10/9/11 at 200K (net −1). The net deficit does shrink from 200 to 1K/200K, which is the basis for the paper's claim that retrieval "effectively approximates oracle skill selection" — but by its own numbers that's a persistent small deficit that narrows, not one that closes or reverses.

A separate structural analysis of the generated DAGs (node count, edge count, max width, max depth, aggregated over all 30 tasks and all three ecosystem sizes) confirms the three orchestration strategies do what their names promise: Quality-First produces the largest, deepest graphs; Efficiency-First keeps a similar node count but favors width over depth (more parallelism); Simplicity-First produces the fewest nodes, shallowest depth, and fewest edges. Three qualitative case studies (an interactive space-exploration webpage, a calculus derivatives teaching package with a Manim-rendered animation and PDF handout, and a quantum-computing slide deck) show what those Bradley-Terry numbers correspond to concretely: the vanilla baseline produces functional but visually plain deliverables — small static images, unstyled matplotlib plots, text-heavy slides — while Quality-First composes image-generation, animation, and presentation skills into polished, professionally designed outputs.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The headline comparison here is entirely in-house: Vanilla, w/ Full Pool, w/ Retrieval, and w/ Oracle Skills are all the same Claude Code Agent SDK running claude-sonnet-4.5 with different skill-provisioning strategies, and all three AgentSkillOS orchestration variants use claude-opus-4.5 to build the tree, retrieve, and orchestrate, with claude-sonnet-4.5 executing each DAG node. There is no comparison against an actual alternative orchestration framework — not ToolLLM's, HuggingGPT's, or a general multi-agent system's approach to composing several capabilities — despite the paper positioning AgentSkillOS against exactly that literature in its related work. Every baseline in the results section is a stripped-down version of AgentSkillOS's own pipeline, so the paper demonstrates that its components help each other, not that its approach beats the field.

The judge is also claude-opus-4.5 — the same model used to build AgentSkillOS's capability tree and DAG plans in the first place. LLM-as-judge self-preference (a model favoring outputs shaped by its own family's reasoning style) is a well-documented failure mode in pairwise evaluation, and the paper reports no check for it: no human-agreement study, no second judge model, no measurement of how often the two presentation orders actually disagreed before being folded into a tie. Given that the entire ranking is built from this one judge's pairwise calls, that's a real gap in an otherwise careful position-bias-mitigation design (swap testing is done, but only for order, not for judge identity).

The oracle-approximation claim is also a place where the prose runs ahead of the numbers. "Tree-based retrieval effectively approximates oracle skill selection" is true in the sense that the deficit shrinks (net win-loss margin against Quality-First (Oracle) goes from −4 to −1 to −1 as |S| grows from 200 to 1K to 200K), but Quality-First loses more comparisons than it wins against the oracle variant at every single ecosystem size tested — the deficit narrows, it doesn't close. A reader skimming the prose alone would come away thinking retrieval is nearly solved; the underlying win/tie/loss counts say it's a persistent, if shrinking, gap.

The benchmark itself is small (30 tasks, six per category) and the 200-skill pool — the condition every method is evaluated on first — is deliberately seeded with "the best-performing skill for each benchmark task" plus hand-picked high-quality extras, rather than an organic slice of the real, messy 280K-skill marketplace; only the 1K and 200K pools are extended by raw install-count. That's applied identically across all methods, so it isn't an unfair advantage for AgentSkillOS specifically, but it does mean the smallest, easiest condition is not representative of the decentralized, heterogeneous ecosystem the paper's own motivation describes.

A reader coming to this page for the benchmark itself, rather than the framework, should also know: it is never given a name anywhere in the paper's fifteen pages — it's called only "a benchmark" or "our benchmark," never a proper noun a citation could hang on — and it isn't released as a standalone artifact; the only URL the paper gives for its own materials is the AgentSkillOS GitHub repository, with no separate dataset link or license statement. The paper frames its construction instrumentally, twice, rather than as a first-class contribution in its own right: "To evaluate the agent's ability to invoke skills, we construct a benchmark" (abstract) and "To systematically evaluate AgentSkillOS, we construct a benchmark of 30 tasks" (Sec. 1). It earns its own related-work comparison against ToolLLM, API-Bank, Gorilla, and the concurrent SkillsBench, but as written it is this paper's evaluation harness first and a reusable community benchmark second.

baselines

All baselines are ablations of AgentSkillOS's own pipeline on the same Claude Code Agent SDK backbone; no external orchestration framework or non-Claude skill/tool system is compared.

contamination

Not really applicable in the usual training-data sense — the benchmark is newly authored, human-crafted tasks — but the judge model (claude-opus-4.5) is the same model family used to build the tree and DAGs being judged, an analogous self-evaluation concern the paper doesn't address.

what's missed

No human-preference validation of the LLM judge; no reporting of how often the two swapped orderings actually disagreed (vs. how many ties came from genuine quality parity); no confidence intervals on the fitted Bradley-Terry scores from only 24 (Table 1) or 30 (ablation) judged comparisons per cell.

would raise confidence

A human-agreement check on the pairwise judge; a second, different judge model; at least one non-AgentSkillOS orchestration baseline; and an explanation for why w/ Full Pool's score rose from 200 to 1K skills before collapsing at 200K, rather than declining monotonically as the "invisible skills" story would predict.

// bottom line

The ablation is genuinely informative — it isolates retrieval from orchestration and shows both matter, including the sharp finding that handing the flat Claude Code agent the exact oracle skill set still isn't enough without DAG structure. But the evaluation is a closed loop: one Claude model builds the plans, another Claude model executes them, and a third Claude model judges the result, with no outside baseline or human check anywhere in that chain. Treat the headline Bradley-Terry numbers as evidence that AgentSkillOS's two components help each other, not as a validated claim about how it stacks up against the broader agent-orchestration field.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. AgentSkillOS separates skill management — an offline capability tree built once via recursive LLM categorization, with a usage-frequency queue that, at the largest tested scale (200K skills), keeps only the top 10,000 in the active tree and pushes the rest into a dormant index — from skill use — per-task retrieval plus DAG-based orchestration — so retrieval scales by walking a hierarchy instead of searching flat over the whole ecosystem.
  2. The paper's ablation shows orchestration structure matters independently of skill selection: handing the flat, unstructured Claude Code Agent SDK the exact oracle skill set (w/ Oracle Skills) still loses decisively to the same skills organized into a DAG (Quality-First wins 17-19 of 30 comparisons against it at every scale tested: 18/6/6 at |S|=200, 17/7/6 at 1K, 19/3/8 at 200K).
  3. Native flat skill provisioning doesn't scale on its own: w/ Full Pool's Bradley-Terry score collapses to 17.2 at |S|=200K (down from 48.1 at 1K), which the paper attributes to skills becoming effectively invisible to the agent as the pool grows — but the whole evaluation, including that claim, rests on a single closed loop of Claude models building, executing, and judging the results, with no external baseline or human check.
